title: The resurrection of the body
hookLine: the Creed ends with the body raised
tomorrow: so what is heaven like, if Paul says no eye has seen it?

lines: THE FEED, OR JUST A SHELL?
cards: Bodies are all over your feed: the glow-up, the workout split, the skincare shelf. Then at a funeral someone says the body was just a shell; the real person is gone somewhere else. The Creed takes a third road.
The Apostles' Creed ends: I believe in the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Not the soul's escape. The body.
And Luke adds a strange detail. The risen Jesus asks his friends for something to eat, and they hand him a piece of broiled fish. Why tell us about the fish?

teach.h: NOT A GHOST: FLESH AND BONES.
teach.b: Luke's answer is in the verse before. The disciples think they're seeing a ghost.
Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "See my hands and feet, that it is I myself; handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have."
Then he eats in front of them. The fish is the proof. Whatever rising from the dead is, it isn't floating free of a body.
Now a second puzzle. Paul says the dead are raised with a spiritual body. Isn't that a contradiction?
You plant a bare seed, and what comes up isn't the seed, but it isn't something else either. "It is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body."

The same you, changed, no longer able to die. Paul even lists the changes: sown in weakness, it rises in power; sown without honor, it rises in glory. That's why Catholics treat the bodies of the dead with such care.
Here's one to tell a friend: the Creed doesn't end with your soul going up. It ends with your body getting up.
The hands you have now are part of the promise.

how: Catholics profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed at Mass and bury their dead with reverence, in hope of the resurrection.

games.q: what does “the resurrection of the body” mean?
o: the dead raised bodily, changed, at the end of time
the soul leaving the body behind for good at death
the body kept whole so that it never decays

games.q: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.
p: proof the risen Jesus wasn't a ghost
Paul's picture: the same, yet changed

s: Catholics believe only the soul lives on after death
the Creed ends with the resurrection of the body: the whole person, raised.
in Luke, the risen Jesus eats in front of his disciples
broiled fish, so they'd know he wasn't a ghost.
Paul says the raised body is exactly like this one
sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body: the same, but changed.

games.q: your little brother asks if grandpa will need his glasses after the resurrection. what answer fits the Creed and Paul's seed?
o: grandpa will be himself, raised and changed, like a seed becomes a plant.
grandpa won't have a body at all, only a soul floating free.
everyone comes back exactly as they were the day they died.
games.why: the Creed promises the body raised, and Paul says changed: the same person, no longer able to die. the glasses are anyone's guess.

practice: Look at your hands, palms up, then turned over, slowly, as if you'd never seen them before. Every scar, every knuckle, the calluses from whatever you do.
Stay with them until the bell, and if you pray, you can thank God for them as they are.

wordCard.voice: The resurrection of the body. The Creed's last promise: not escape from the body, but the body raised, changed and alive.

orig.note: Greek: resurrection, a standing up again. the New Testament's word for rising from the dead.

carryVoice: Keep this one: these hands, the same you, raised and not swapped out. Until tomorrow.
